[1v] [Siddham] Homage to the illustrious Remover of Obstacles!
Possessing knowledge comparable to the great illusion manifested in forms arising from the three worlds;
bearing the ground of the dharmadhātu which follows the vajra of speech;
and removing the torment of the suffering of worldly existence with sprays of the nectar of compassion.
May the illustrious one, who acts for the welfare of the world, bring about the fulfillment of all your aims.
With a mind filled with the joy born from the touch of the heart by the pollen of the lotus feet of Śrī Vajradharma,
[he established] the tenfold office of ritual action residing in the scriptures.
It is explained out of consideration for the students. || 0 ||
Now, the consecration is examined:

the statement of its virtues and defects, the restoration of the dilapidated, and the festival of the banner; [is it not the raising of the banner? In the *Anna* [text], there is the raising of the banner.
The laying of bricks for the site-dragon occurs in the forest; the birthplace of the dragon arising from timber is there. || O ||
But is it not so?
All phenomena are by their very nature primordially peaceful and unarisen.
But in the investigation of ultimate reality, who stands where, and by what means?
[How] are those that are unproduced from the very beginning established? How, and in what manner, do they abide? [...]
When analyzed from the perspective of ultimate reality, what is established by whom, and where?
Buddhas are present everywhere, yet they are not established anywhere;
like space, how can they be said to have a foundation?
All Buddhas are perfectly present, yet there is no place where they abide.
While they dwell everywhere like space, they are conceptualized as "the other" by those who are dualistic.
And it is said:
For the sake of beings who are beginners, the purification of causes and actions was established by the Victors based upon worldly convention.
Relying [upon this], it serves merely as a cause for the realization of sentient beings who are beginners in their practice. [...
Relying upon worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), one establishes and thoroughly investigates [the ultimate].
And furthermore:
Where a completed image remains for a long time unpūjita,
misfortune arises there as long as that pūjā does not take place.
If a complete image remains for a long time without having been consecrated, inauspiciousness will arise therein; it is not fit to be worshipped for as long as that is the case.
*Pūjitā vanditā vātha pratimā tv apratiṣṭhitā* (An image that has not been consecrated should not be worshipped or venerated).
Just as an oblation offered without the proper mantra into ashes is fruitless, so too [is that which is performed without the mantra].
Whoever offers worship and prostrations to an image that has not been consecrated—

being devoid of the samaya and deficient in mantra— their burnt offering will be as fruitless as ashes. One must indeed perform the consecration of the Buddha and others according to the prescribed ritual.
Why [is it] not according to the injunctions? That which is devoid of injunction is not excellent; it is censured in both worlds.
The consecration of the Buddha and so forth should be performed according to the ritual procedures;
it must not be done with deficient rituals, for a consecration performed improperly is always inauspicious.
It brings suffering in this world and great fear in the next.
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment should perform [the ritual] with every effort,
according to the procedure taught in the *Kalpatantra*, through the application of oneself.
Through one's own true power, O Mother,
one should exert oneself with all diligence, desiring the attainment of siddhi;
according to the excellent method taught in the *Kalpa*, by means of the ritual capacity of the self.
Thus, because of the scriptural teaching. ||o||
[1. Sthāpana] Having thoroughly purified that site and having diligently extracted any splinters,
one should then examine and discard nails, bones, hair, wood, and so forth.
One should divide the ground plot of the temple into nine parts;
indeed, the northeast and southeast corners are the auspicious portions belonging to the deity.
The upper portion belongs to the Daityas; the left and right sides belong to humans;
the lower portion is the share of the Pretas in the southwest; and the rear portion belongs to the denizens of hell.
In the intermediate directions, the northwest corner consists of twelve sections, while the center has nine; having raised this up with sand, one should fill it.
Having struck it level and made it even across its full extent,
one should [draw] in order from east to south in a clockwise rotation upon the base of the seat.
One should place a vessel of nectar below, not touching [the base],
made of gold, silver, jewels, or copper, pure,
consisting of five, one, or nine according to the extent of one's wealth.
Surely, in accordance with one's capacity,
for the sake of purifying the intellect through the expansion of non-dual knowledge.

With blue-lotus-colored emeralds, with topazes that have stolen the luster of the sun, and with those whose interiors are manifested as the seed-syllables of the Jinas according to the colors of the directions;
and with gold produced from milk, clarified butter, sugar-candy, molasses, and honey—
With camphor, saffron, excellent sandalwood, musk, and sihlaka;
Having thoroughly filled it with *pārāra* resin and bound its opening,
one should place it there after consecrating it one hundred and eight times with the *devahṛdaya* mantra; or alternatively, having placed it within a vessel made of gold, silver, or lotus-leaf.
One should place the jewels in the proper sequence of the Tathāgatas.
[He is] the Meru-jewel arisen from the ocean of the water of knowledge and the fire of digestion produced by the spreading wind of the stomach;
his interior purified by the rays of the lotus, the sun, the moon, and the thunderbolt.
Having attained the peak posture, he rises upward.

One should cause [the structure] to rise with a height equal to twice the width of one part, situated upon a seat that has a width of three parts multiplied by the extent of the portion of the deity and a height of one and a half parts;
its width and breadth being two parts and its height one part.
Its extent in human measures is four and a half [yojanas].
It may be made of stone, gold, silver, copper, or brick;
it should be provided with three, two, or one girdle, and be square or otherwise shaped; it should be well-proportioned according to the rules of the arts and adorned with lions and other ornaments.
Exceedingly beautiful in every limb, and variegated with jewels.
One should contemplate twelvefold through the resolute conviction in the stages of wisdom and gnosis,
just as the Supreme Buddha did in the *Śrīvajramaṇḍalālaṅkāra Tantra*.

The sixth is known by the name Padmaprabhā, who shines forth beautifully like a lotus.
Because its nature is pure by its very essence, it is stainless and free from grasping.
The sixth is named Padmadhara; she is as brilliantly radiant as a lotus.
By her very nature, the *dharmatā* is pure, devoid of self and free from grasping.
The seventh is known by the name Karmaprabhā, the one who brings about the qualities of a Buddha.
The eighth, however, is named Anupamā; no comparison for it exists therein.
The seventh is called the Stage of Action (*karmabhūmi*), where the Buddha’s enlightened activities are performed;
the eighth is called the Incomparable (*anupama*), for no comparison exists for it; the ninth is named the Peerless (*nirupamā*), which penetrates the illusion-like nature of reality.
The tenth, named the Radiance of Wisdom (*prajñāprabhā*), is the unsurpassed stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), which is beyond compare.

The ninth is called "Beyond Similes," in which all similes are fully engaged; the tenth is called "Light of Wisdom," the unsurpassed Buddha-ground. The eleventh is the great stage known as "Well-Known," which is luminous.
The twelfth [day] is to be realized within oneself; it fulfills the knowledge of the yogis.
The eleventh is called "Omniscience itself," and the great stage is "Luminosity. The twelfth is "Individual Self-Awareness," the complete perfection of yogic gnosis;

[2. Discussion of Qualities and Faults] One should examine the qualities and faults of the deities being installed.
Through virtue arises excellence; through fault, the birth of the inauspicious.
Slightly lower than that, the Bimba [mandala], very firm through the deities and the Victors,
bestows upon sentient beings the perfection of all desired aims and objects.
Sovereignty over the Dharma, personal valor, good fortune, honor and worship, victory, worship,
great contentment, success in trade, and freedom from dispute.
Or, established in his human portion, he brings about the increase of sons and daughters,
as well as the abundance of wealth, kinsmen, wives, female slaves, and male servants.

An image made of stone bestows kingdom, wealth, and strength; one made of iron destroys enemies;
while those made of tin and lead grant success in minor rites of malevolent magic.
An arrow made of three metals (trailoha) brings death; one made of five metals (pāñcaloha) brings wealth;
and one made entirely of iron is recommended for all purposes, bestowing success and the fulfillment of every desire.
Copper bestows the increase of sons and other blessings; bell-metal grants eradication and liberation; lead brings about nourishment; and silver accomplishes peace.
An image made of bell-metal or gold bestows all prosperity, enjoyment, and liberation;
an image of the Lord made of all kinds of gems grants all prosperity and liberation.
The crystal [image] is known to be enchanting and to increase the power of wisdom;
a painting situated on cloth or a wall bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.

a deity made of fine clay bestows longevity, prosperity, strength, and liberation.
